Title: Online sexual abuse victims face uphill legal battle in China

Summary: 
A Telegram channel called 'MaskPark', which had hundreds of thousands of subscribers, circulated revenge porn and hidden‑camera videos of Chinese women. The channel was shut down by Telegram, but activists say alternate channels have already emerged and only some are removed. Activist and researcher Li Ling explained that the absence of a specific offence means police officers do not know how to file a case, and that to sue, the perpetrator’s identity is required – but Telegram does not verify users and is blocked in China, making it impossible to trace the posters. Telegram said it has "completely removed the MaskPark channels" and monitors for new groups. The article references the 2020 South Korean Nth‑room case, where a man received a 40‑year sentence after a journalist infiltrated a Telegram channel. It also cites a 2024 U.S. law signed by President Trump that imposes stricter penalties for distributing non‑consensual videos. In China, a December case saw a college graduate’s deep‑fake porn shared on X; the perpetrator received only 10 days of administrative detention, though the offence can carry up to two years in prison, or three if money was exchanged. Activists Li Maizi and Jiahui Duan argue that the current "disseminating obscene materials" charge is too broad and that systemic solutions are needed.
